submission.natural_language_explanation: L1/H7 writes the layer-1 value of the single token it locks onto - most often the token immediately before it, sometimes the current token itself or the keyword that opened the construct (frac, import, DTD) - so its write is large exactly when that copied token is an unusual, template-anchoring one rather than an everyday English word. Predict active (2-3.5, far above the 0.8 active line) on the token that continues a fixed format keyed by such an anchor: a month name plus day number ('January 26', 'June 4,' - 15/15 dates, 1.9-3.1), a TeX command before its brace ('\frac', '\sqrt'), a code keyword or declaration before its arguments (import, include, SELECT, <!DOCTYPE, 2.4-3.5), all-caps licence boilerplate (WARRANTY, GNU, 2.1-2.9), a courtesy opener ('Thanks', 'Thank you'), and on any token of non-Latin-script text (Bengali, Tamil, Thai, Hindi, Korean, Japanese, Greek, Russian, 1.6-2.7); predict inactive (below 0.6) on a whole text that is only comma-separated integers (15/15, 0.06-0.58) or only the most frequent English function words; this is a broad head on prose, whose peak usually crosses only weakly (0.8-1.5) where it locks onto an ordinary content word.

rival_explanations: The head is a generic rare-token copy head rather than a template head: any unusual, capitalised or technical token immediately before the position should fire it, so a single proper noun or acronym in plain prose ('The Franklin report was long', 'The Quasar project failed') would activate it as strongly as a date or a TeX command, which my probes put at only 0.5-1.3.

The strong activations are essentially a script effect: the head copies whatever token came last, so outside non-Latin text it is a plain previous-token detector and the English date, code and TeX peaks are just the rare words that happen to precede the peak - predicting that a comma-separated integer list or common-word prose with a preceding content word would be as active as 'January 26'.
